chapters.title: Chapter 1: What an Economic Moat Really Is

lessons.title: Why Moats Drive Long-Term Shareholder Returns

body.text: In the short run, share prices follow sentiment and valuation. Over ten or twenty years, they follow earnings. A moat is what keeps earnings compounding long enough for that to matter.

children.text: The first three lessons defined a moat and showed how to spot its fingerprint in ROCE. This lesson answers the question every investor eventually asks: does any of this actually show up in my portfolio returns? It does, but only if you understand where stock returns come from and how long you hold.
Where Stock Returns Come From
Every rupee of return from owning a stock comes from just three sources.

body.caption: An approximation for annual returns. Over multiple years the first two compound together: Price change = EPS growth factor × P/E change factor.

children.text: EPS growth:
how fast profit per share rises. This is driven by ROCE and reinvestment, exactly what a moat protects.
Change in P/E:
how much more or less the market is willing to pay for each rupee of earnings. This is driven by sentiment, interest rates, and expectations.
Dividend yield:
cash paid out along the way.
The key insight is that
P/E changes are bounded

. A multiple can go from 50 to 25 or from 10 to 20, but it cannot keep halving or doubling forever. Earnings growth, if protected by a moat, has no such ceiling. So the longer you hold, the more earnings growth dominates your result.

body.label: The Munger principle (paraphrased)
body.value: Over long periods, a stock's return tends to converge towards the return on capital the underlying business earns
body.context: Charlie Munger made this point repeatedly: buy a business earning 6% on capital and you will struggle to do much better than 6% over decades, even if you buy cheaply.

children.text: A 20-Year Thought Experiment
Two hypothetical NSE-listed companies. You invest ₹1 lakh in each today and hold for 20 years. Ignore dividends to keep the comparison clean.

Everything about the valuation works against Moat Co. You paid a steep price, and the multiple shrinks. Everything works for No-Moat Co. You bought cheaply, and the multiple expands. Here is what happens.

body.title: Illustrative: Value of ₹100 Invested, P/E Changing Gradually

children.text: Moat Co: EPS growth factor over 20 years = 1.15^20 = 16.37. P/E change factor = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60. Price change factor = 16.37 × 0.60 = 9.82. ₹1 lakh becomes ₹9.82 lakh. CAGR = 9.82^(1/20) − 1 ≈ 12.1%.
No-Moat Co: EPS growth factor = 1.06^20 = 3.21. P/E change factor = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.50. Price change factor = 3.21 × 1.50 = 4.81. ₹1 lakh becomes ₹4.81 lakh. CAGR = 4.81^(1/20) − 1 ≈ 8.2%.
The chart assumes each P/E moves in a straight line between its starting and ending value: Moat Co falls by one turn a year, No-Moat Co rises by a quarter turn a year.
But Watch What Happens Over Three Years
Now suppose the entire valuation shift happens quickly, within the first three years, which is common when a market cools on expensive quality stocks or a cheap stock gets rediscovered.

body.caption: Same companies, same P/E changes, very different horizons

cells: No-Moat Co, by a wide margin
Moat Co, ending with about twice the wealth

children.text: Over three years, Moat Co's 15% earnings growth (1.15^3 = 1.52) is wiped out by a 40% derating, leaving you with a loss. No-Moat Co's modest 6% growth (1.06^3 = 1.19) combined with a 50% rerating produces a spectacular return. An investor judging on a three-year window would conclude moats do not matter. An investor with a twenty-year window would conclude the opposite. Both are looking at the same two businesses.

body.text: Moats reward patience, not trading. If your holding period is short, valuation and sentiment will dominate your returns. The moat advantage only shows up once enough years of compounding have accumulated to overwhelm the change in multiple.

body.title: Split the Return
body.prompt: A company's EPS triples over 10 years. Over the same period its P/E falls from 40x to 20x. Ignoring dividends, by what percentage has the share price risen in total over the 10 years?
body.explanation: Price change factor = EPS factor × P/E factor = 3 × (20 ÷ 40) = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5. The share price is 1.5 times where it started, a total rise of 50%. Earnings did most of the work; the halving of the P/E took most of it back.

children.text: Three More Ways Moats Help Shareholders
1. Fewer Permanent Losses

A temporary fall in price is recoverable. A permanent collapse in earning power is not. No-moat businesses are far more likely to see profits disappear for good when a stronger competitor arrives, as Indian telecom incumbents found after Jio launched in 2016. Moat businesses can still fall sharply in a market crash, but their earnings tend to recover.
2. Growth That Does Not Need Constant Fundraising
High ROCE means a company can fund expansion from its own cash flows. Low-ROCE businesses often need repeated equity raises or more debt to grow, which dilutes existing shareholders or adds risk.
3. Cash Returned When Reinvestment Runs Out

Some moat businesses cannot reinvest all their profits at high returns because their market is mature. Hindustan Unilever and Nestle India, for example, have historically paid out a large share of profits as dividends. Shareholders still benefit, through a steady and growing dividend stream instead of rapid reinvestment.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: Over short holding periods, changes in the P/E multiple tend to dominate returns. Over long holding periods, growth in ___ tends to dominate.
body.explanation: P/E multiples are bounded and tend to revert, but protected earnings growth keeps compounding. That is why the moat advantage becomes visible mainly over long horizons.

body.title: The Frustrated Quality Investor
body.scenario: Priya, a salaried professional in Pune, bought shares of a well-known consumer company with a clear moat at 70x earnings in 2021. Three years later, the company's earnings have grown about 13% a year, but the stock has barely moved because the P/E has fallen to around 48x. Her colleague made 60% in the same period on a cyclical PSU stock bought at 6x earnings. Priya is thinking of selling and buying the PSU stock.
body.prompt: Using what you learned in this lesson, explain what happened to Priya's investment and what she should consider before switching.
body.modelAnswer: Priya's return was split between two forces pulling in opposite directions. Earnings grew roughly 1.13^3 = 1.44 times, but the P/E fell from 70x to 48x, a factor of about 0.69, so the share price ended close to 1.44 × 0.69 = 0.99 times where she bought it. The business did its job; the valuation she paid took it back. Her colleague's gain came mostly from a rerating of a cheap cyclical, which is not repeatable indefinitely. Before switching, Priya should ask: Is the moat still intact, with ROCE and margins holding up? Is 48x still demanding, or now closer to reasonable for the growth on offer? What is the PSU company's ROCE across a full cycle, and can its multiple keep rising? If the moat is intact and the valuation has become less stretched, the three-year disappointment may have improved her forward odds. The real lesson is about entry price, which Chapter 7 covers in detail.

body.text: None of this means any price is fine for a moat business. The thought experiment shows that a great business can overcome an expensive starting valuation over 20 years. It does not show that it always will, or that it will over your holding period. Overpaying remains the most common way investors turn a great business into a poor investment.

cards.definition: A fall in the P/E multiple the market is willing to pay, which lowers the share price even if earnings are unchanged.
A rise in the P/E multiple, which lifts the share price even if earnings are unchanged.
Compound annual growth rate: (Ending value ÷ Starting value)^(1/years) − 1.
A loss that does not recover because the business's earning power has been lost, as opposed to a temporary price fall.

body.text: Moat Co, No-Moat Co, and the Priya scenario are hypothetical and for illustration only. Companies named are examples of concepts, not recommendations.

points: Stock returns come from EPS growth, changes in the P/E multiple, and dividends
P/E changes are bounded, while moat-protected earnings growth can compound for decades
In the 20-year example, a moat business bought at 50x and derating to 30x still beat a no-moat business bought at 10x that rerated to 15x: roughly 12.1% vs 8.2% CAGR
Over three years, the same valuation shifts made the no-moat business look far better, so the moat advantage needs time to show
Moats also reduce permanent loss of capital, reduce reliance on fundraising, and support dividends when reinvestment runs out
A great business can still be a poor investment if you overpay, which is the focus of Chapter 7
